'''bronzing-machine''' (bron′zing-ma̤-shēn″), ''n.'' A machine for decorating wall-papers, fabrics, labels, etc., with bronze-powder.

'''bronzist''' (bron′zist), ''n.'' [< ''bronze'' + ''-ist.''] One who casts bronzes, or works in bronze.

'''bronzite''' (bron′zīt), ''n.'' [< ''bronze'' + ''-ite''<sup>1</sup>.] A ferriferous variety of the mineral enstatite, having sometimes a submetallic bronze-like luster due to microscopic inclusions.

'''bronzy''' (bron′zi), ''a.'' [< ''bronze'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Resembling bronze: as, a ''bronzy'' appearance.
{{smaller block|The Cicindela maritima, which is found only on sandy sea-shores, is of a pale ''bronzy'' yellow, so as to be almost invisible.
{{right|''A. R. Wallace'', Nat. Select., p. 57.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bronze|694|brook}}</noinclude>resembling bronze; bronze-powder.—'''4.''' Boldness; impudence; brass.
{{smaller block|<poem>Imbrown’d with native ''bronze'', lo! Henley stands,
Tuning his voice, and balancing his hands.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, iii. 199.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Amber bronze.''' See ''amber''<sup>2</sup>.—'''Bavarian bronze.''' See ''Bavarian''.—'''Chemical bronze,''' nitromuriate of platinum, an efficient but expensive bronzing liquid.—'''Malleable bronze,''' an alloy of copper and tin which contains in addition ½ to 2 per cent. of mercury.—'''Manganese bronze,''' an alloy formed by the addition of from 1 to 2 per cent. of manganese to the proportions of copper and zinc used in making brass.—'''White bronze,''' a generic name given to the lighter bronzes which approach the color of tin.}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Made of or resembling bronze: as, a ''bronze'' statue.—'''2.''' Characterized by the use of bronze: as, the ''bronze'' age.—{{smaller|'''Bronze age.''' See ''archæological ages'', under ''age''.—'''Bronze coloring,''' surface effects resembling those of bronzes, produced either directly by application of color to the surface, or indirectly by changes due to the action of acids, salts, and coloring matter. See ''bronzing''.—'''Bronze green.''' See ''green''.—'''Bronze turkey,''' a large variety of domestic turkey with dark-brown plumage having a brilliant metallic luster.}}

'''bronze''' (bronz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bronzed'', ppr. ''bronzing''.   [= F. ''bronzer'' = Sp. ''broncear'', OSp. ''bronzar'' = Pg. ''bronzear'', bronze; cf. It. ''abbronzare'', tan, scorch, sunburn, imbrown; from the noun.]   '''1.''' To make brown or of the color of bronze, as by exposure to the sun.
{{smaller block|<poem>Seam’d with an ancient swordcut on the cheek,
And bruised and ''bronzed''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
{{smaller block|His face was ''bronzed'' as though by burning climes.
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 414.}}}}
'''2.''' To give the color or appearance of bronze to, as by applying copper-dust or -leaf to the surface, etc.—'''3.''' To harden or make like bronze; hence, figuratively, to make hard or unfeeling.
{{smaller block|The lawyer who ''bronzes'' his bosom instead of his forehead.
{{right|''Scott.''}}}}

'''bronze-backer''' (bronz′bak″ėr), ''n.'' A name given to the black-bass.
{{smaller block|''Bronze-backer'' is one of its pet names among the anglers.
{{right|''Goode'', American Fishes.}}}}

'''bronzed''' (bronzd), ''p. a.'' Colored by bronzing; of a bronze color; tanned.—{{smaller|'''Bronzed glass''', ornamental glass of dark-green paste, which has been exposed to corrosive vapors, so that the surface is iridescent when seen by reflected light.—'''Bronzed-skin disease.''' Same as ''Addison’s disease'' (which see, under ''disease'').}}

'''bronze-gold''' (bronz′gōld), ''n.'' A name given to all the so-called bronzes which have a golden color.

'''bronze-liquid''' (bronz′lik″wid), ''n.'' A kind of varnish mixed with bronze-powder to make bronze-paint.

'''bronze-liquor''' (bronz′lik″o̤r), ''n.'' A solution of antimony chlorid and copper sulphate, used for bronzing gun-barrels, etc.

'''bronze-paint''' (bronz′pānt), ''n.'' A pigment consisting of bronze-powder with varnish as a vehicle. Commonly called ''gold-paint.''

'''bronze-powder''' (bronz′pou″dėr), ''n.'' A pigment made by reducing leaves of Dutch metal or some similar alloy, to powder. {{smaller|The color is varied as may be desired from pale-yellow to deep-red, by using different proportions of the component metals, copper and zinc.}}

'''bronzewing''' (bronz′wing), ''n.'' A name for certain species of Australian pigeons, chiefly of the genus ''Phaps'', distinguished by the bronze color of their plumage. {{smaller|The common bronze-winged ground-dove, ''P. chalcoptera'', abounds in all the Australian colonies, and is a plump bird, often weighing a pound, much esteemed for the table.}}

'''bronzify''' (bron′zi-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bronzified'', ppr. ''bronzifying''.   [< ''bronze'' + ''-i-fy''.]   To make like bronze; cast in bronze; represent in a bronze figure or statue.
{{smaller block|St. Michael descending upon the Fiend has been caught and ''bronzified'' just as he lighted on the castle of St. Angelo.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, xxxv.}}}}

'''bronzine''' (bron′zin), ''a.''   [= It. ''bronzino'', bronzed, sunburnt (cf. ML. ''bronzinus'', n., bronze); < ''bronze'' + ''-ine''<sup>1</sup>.]   Resembling bronze; bronze-colored.

'''bronzing''' (bron′zing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''bronze'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The process of giving a bronze-like surface to metals, plaster, wood, and other substances. {{smaller|This is commonly effected by the application of a liquid called ''chemical bronze'', a solution of the chlorid (nitromuriate) of platinum; it may also be done by the electrotype process, or by dusting with a bronze-powder any surface which has been rubbed with linseed-oil varnish.}} '''2.''' A metallic color or iridescent appearance as of bronze.
{{smaller block|By this time the dark shadows ought to show the greenish, almost metallic look known as ''bronzing''.
{{right|''Lea'', Photography, p. 45.}}}}
'''Bronzing-salt''', {{smaller|antimony chlorid, so called because it is}} used in the process of browning gun-barrels and other articles of iron: bronze-liquor.

'''bronzing-machine''' (bron′zing-ma̤-shēn″), ''n.'' A machine for decorating wall-papers, fabrics, labels, etc., with bronze-powder.

'''bronzist''' (bron′zist), ''n.''   [< ''bronze'' + ''-ist.'']   One who casts bronzes, or works in bronze.

'''bronzite''' (bron′zīt), ''n.''   [< ''bronze'' + ''-ite''<sup>1</sup>.]   A ferriferous variety of the mineral enstatite, having sometimes a submetallic bronze-like luster due to microscopic inclusions.

'''bronzy''' (bron′zi), ''a.''   [< ''bronze'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Resembling bronze: as, a ''bronzy'' appearance.
{{smaller block|The Cicindela maritima, which is found only on sandy sea-shores, is of a pale ''bronzy'' yellow, so as to be almost invisible.
{{right|''A. R. Wallace'', Nat. Select., p. 57.}}}}

'''broo<sup>1</sup>''' (brö), ''n.'' Same as ''bree''<sup>1</sup>.

'''broo<sup>2</sup>''' (brö), ''n.'' See ''brow'', 11.

'''brooch<sup>1</sup>''' (brōch or bröch), ''n.''   [Same as ''broach'', q. v., ''brooch'' being the commoner spelling of the word in this sense.]   An ornamental clasp consisting of a pin and a projecting or covering shield, used for fastening the dress, or merely for display. {{smaller|When the garment is large and heavy, as a cloak or the ecclesiastical cope, the brooch has generally been found insufficient, and has been replaced by the agraffe or some other form of clasp. Ornamental brooches are now worn mostly by women, but were formerly worn by both sexes, sometimes on the hat or cap. Also spelled ''broach''.}}
{{smaller block|He has a wide beard and flowing yellow hair; a green cloak wrapped around him; a bright silver ''brooch'' in his cloak over his breast.
{{right|Quoted by ''W. K. Sullivan'', Introd. to O’Curry’s Anc. [Irish, p. ccccxlvi.}}}}
{{smaller block|With ''broches'' and aiglets of gold upon their caps.
{{right|''R. Robinson'', tr. of Sir T. More’s Utopia, ii. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|Honour ’s a good ''brooch'' to wear in a man’s hat at all times.
{{right|''B. Jonson.''}}}}

[[File:century v01 p0720 c2f1.png|center|351px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Brooch of the Merovingian period, found at St. Denis and now in the Musée de Cluny, Paris. (From “Dict. du Mobilier français.”)}}}}

'''brooch'''<sup>1</sup> (brōch or bröch), ''v. t.''   [< ''brooch''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   To adorn with or as with a brooch or brooches. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Not the imperious show
Of the full-fortun’d Cæsar ever shall
Be ''brooch’d'' with me. ''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 13.</poem>}}

'''brooch'''<sup>2</sup> (brōch), ''n.''   [Origin uncertain.]   A monotint, or picture in one color, as a sepia sketch.

'''brood'''<sup>1</sup> (bröd), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brood'', ''brod'', < AS. ''brōd'' (= D. ''broed'' = MLG. ''brot'' = OHG. MHG. ''bruot'', G. ''brut''), brood; with formative ''-d'', from the same root (*''brō'', warm, heat) as G. ''brühe'', broth: see ''broil''<sup>1</sup>. Hence ''breed'', q. v.]   '''1.''' Offspring; progeny.
{{smaller block|The lion roars and gluts his tawny ''brood''. {{right|''Wordsworth.''}}}}
'''2.''' A hatch; the young birds hatched in one nest, or those placed together in the care of one hen, or in an artificial brooder: as, a ''brood'' of chickens or of ducks.—'''3.''' That which is bred; species generated; that which is produced; hence, figuratively, sort or kind.
{{smaller block|<poem>Have you forgotten Libya’s burning wastes, . . .
Its tainted air, and all its ''broods'' of poison?</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Cato.}}}}
'''4.''' In ''mining'', any heterogeneous mixture with tin or copper ore, as mundic or black-jack. ''R. Hunt.''—'''5.''' A north of Scotland name for salmon-fry.—{{smaller|'''Ants’ brood.''' See ''ant''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To sit on brood†''', to be in the act of brooding, like a bird sitting on eggs; figuratively, to ponder.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There’s something in his soul,
O’er which his melancholy ''sits on brood.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' ''Covey'', etc. See ''flock''.}}

'''brood'''<sup>1</sup> (bröd), ''v.''   [< ME. ''broden'', brood (< ''brod'', brood), equiv. to the earlier ''breden'', breed: see ''breed'', ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To sit persistently on eggs, covering and warming them with the body and wings, for the purpose of hatching them: said of birds.
{{smaller block|''Brodyn'', as byrdys, foveo, fetifico. ''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 53.
<poem>Thou from the first
Wast present, and with mighty wings outspread
Dove-like sat’st ''brooding'' on the vast abyss.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 21.}}}}
'''2.''' To rest fixedly like a brooding bird.
{{smaller block|Raven darkness ''brooded'' o’er the deep.
{{right|''Sir W. Jones.''}}}}
'''3.''' To meditate long and anxiously; remain a long time in anxiety or solicitous thought; have the mind dwelling persistently on a subject: with ''on'' or ''over''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Half mad
With exile, and with ''brooding on'' his wrongs.</poem> {{right|''M. Arnold'', Empedocles.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To sit over, cover, and cherish: as, a hen ''broods'' her chicks; hence, to nourish.
{{smaller block|<poem>The thrifty earth that bringeth out
And ''broodeth'' up her breed.</poem>
{{right|''Warner'', Albion’s Eng., ii. 11.}}}}
'''2.''' To cherish with care.
{{smaller block|See how he ''broods'' the boy. {{right|''Fletcher'', Bonduca, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|She ''broods'' and blesses me, she calms and gathers me.
{{right|''E. S. Phelps'', Beyond the Gates, p. 195.}}}}
'''3.''' To ponder over; plan or mature with care: as, “to ''brood'' war,” ''Bacon'', War with Spain.
{{smaller block|You’ll sit and ''brood'' your sorrows on a throne. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''brood<sup>2</sup>†''', ''a.'' An obsolete form of ''broad''.

'''brood-capsule''' (bröd′kap″sūl), ''n.'' A cyst or capsule in which tænia-heads are developed, as an echinococcus (which see).

'''brood-cavity''' (bröd′kav″i̤-ti), ''n.'' A brood-pouch, in general.

'''brood-cell''' (bröd′sel), ''n.'' In ''bee-culture'', a cell of a honeycomb destined for the reception of a larva. {{smaller|The brood-cells are separated from the honey-cells, generally occupying a different comb.}}

'''brooder''' (brö′dėr), ''n.'' A device for the artificial rearing of young chickens or other birds. {{smaller|It consists essentially of an inclosed run, where the young birds are fed, and a covered place for them to run into, which is kept at a temperature of about 90° F., either by means of a lamp placed beneath the metallic floor, or by hot air or water-pipes carried above or below the space occupied by the chicks.}}

'''brooding''' (brö′ding), ''p. a.''   [Ppr. of ''brood''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' Sitting, as a bird on her eggs: as, a ''brooding'' hen.
{{smaller block|<poem>Still did the nightingale
Unto his ''brooding'' mate tell all his tale.</poem> {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 309.}}}}
'''2.''' Warming: as, “the ''brooding'' heat,” ''Tennyson'', Mariana in the South.—'''3.''' Pondering; thinking deeply; disposed to ponder or think deeply: as, a ''brooding'' disposition.
{{smaller block|I could cite many instances where the ''brooding'' humor . . . of our new people long since cropped out in rhyme.
{{right|''Stedman'', Poets of America, p. 59.}}}}
'''4.''' Settled; rooted; fixed in the heart: a figurative use derived from the steadfastness with which a bird sits on her eggs.
{{smaller block|A ''brooding'' and unavowed hostility.
{{right|''Milman'', Latin Christianity, II. ix.}}}}

'''brood-mare''' (bröd′mãr), ''n.'' A mare kept for breeding.

'''brood-pouch''' (bröd′pouch), ''n.'' A pouch, or some similar cavity of the body of an animal, in which eggs or young are received and detained for a time; a brood-cavity.
{{smaller block|He [the male stickleback] only bears the ''brood-pouch'' and alone builds the nest. {{right|''Claus'', Zoölogy (trans.), p. 104.}}}}
{{smaller block|In the Entoprocta there is a peculiar ''brood-pouch.''
{{right|''E. R. Lankester'', Encyc. Brit., XIX. 433.}}}}

'''brood-space''' (bröd′spās), ''n.'' A brood-cavity.
{{smaller block|An egg in the ''brood-space'' formed between the body and the mantle. {{right|''Gegenbaur'', Comp. Anat. (trans.), p. 268.}}}}

'''broody''' (brö′di), ''a.''   [< ME. *''brody'', < AS. ''brōdig'' (= G. ''brütig''), broody, < ''brōd'', brood.]   '''1.''' Of a brooding disposition; inclined to brood or sit, as a hen.
{{smaller block|Tegetmeier states that a cross between two non-sitting varieties [of the common fowl] almost invariably produces a mongrel that becomes ''broody'', and sits with remarkable steadiness.
{{right|''Sir J. Lubbock'', Origin of Civilisation, p. 354.}}}} '''2.''' Breeding or adapted for breeding: as, a ''broody'' bitch.

'''brook<sup>1</sup>''' (bru̇k), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''brooke, broke''; < ME. ''brook, brok,'' < AS. ''brōc,'' a stream, = D. ''broek'' = MLG. ''brōk,'' LG. ''brook,'' a marsh, pool, = OHG. ''brecan,'' etc., break, burst forth: see ''break''.]   A natural stream of water, too small to be called a river.
{{smaller block|Springs make little rivulets; those united make ''brooks;'' and those coming together make rivers, which empty themselves into the sea.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
'''Brook-trout.''' {{smaller|See ''trout.''}}—'''To fly at the brook†.''' {{smaller|See ''fly''<sup>1</sup>.}}

''bruken,'' use, = OHG. ''brūhhan,'' MHG. ''brūchen,'' G. ''brauchen,'' use, need, = Goth. ''brūkjan,'' use, = L.
